A higher-order composite box beam theory is developed to model rectangular beams with arbitrary wall thicknesses.
The theory includes both in-plane and out-of-plane warping deformations and can accurately capture the transverse shear stresses through the thickness of each wall.
The model is used to analyze the structural and aeroelastic performance of high-speed tilt-rotor aircraft blades.
A multidisciplinary optimization procedure is developed to improve the aerodynamic, structural and aeroelastic performance of the tilt-rotor blade.
The objective functions include maximizing the hover figure of merit and the high-speed cruise propulsive efficiency.
Structural, aerodynamic and aeroelastic stability criteria are imposed as constraints on the optimization problem.
The Kreisselmeier-Steinhauser (K-S) function is used to formulate the multiobjective function problem.
A hybrid approximate analysis is used to reduce the computational effort of the optimization.
The optimized design shows significant improvements in the overall performance of the tilt-rotor blade compared to the baseline.
The static and dynamic results of the composite beam theory are validated against experimental data and finite element solutions.
The beam theory can accurately capture the transverse shear stresses and warping deformations in beams with arbitrary wall thicknesses.
The aerodynamic loads are calculated using the classical blade element momentum theory with corrections for the high lift capability of rotor blades.
A procedure is developed for computing the aeroelastic stability of the tilt-rotor blade based on the composite box beam model.
The design variables include the blade planform characteristics and the composite ply orientations of the structural box beam.
The optimization approach is able to find a balanced solution that improves both the hover and high-speed cruise performance.
